title: Mr. F. & Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine
text:
Decision
Mr. F. & Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine
From
Office of the Commissioner for Environmental Information (OCEI)
Case number: OCE-150799-T4L8F4
Published on 9 July 2026
Background
Scope of Review
Analysis And Findings
Decision
Appeal to the High Court
Whether the Department was justified in refusing Part 1 of the request under article 7(5) of the AIE Regulations on the basis that no further relevant information is held by or for it, and in refusing Part 2 under article 9(2)(a) on the basis that the request was manifestly unreasonable having regard to the volume or range of information sought.
9 July 2026
Background
1. This appeal follows a previous decision of this Office in appeal number OCE-147098-T7K4G4, in which the Department’s decision was annulled on the basis that it had failed to give adequate reasons. This Office directed the Department to issue a new internal review decision to the appellant.
2. The AIE request as originally submitted sought:
“a consolidated version of the Code of Best Forest Practice which takes account of any amendments and supplements and identifies elements that have been superseded and by what material they have been superseded.
I suspect that no such document exists and in the absence of a consolidated document the information sought is;
All information which relates to or has the effect of modifying the Code of Best Forest Practice in terms of amendment, supplementation or through effective removal of elements by virtue of superseding them by subsequent policy documents and technical standards and requirements.”
3. On 19 July 2024 the Department issued the following internal review decision to the appellant:
“I have decided to divide this request into two sections namely Part 1: Consolidated version of the Code of Best Practice. Part 2: All information regarding modifying the Code of Best Practice.
Part 1: My decision is to annul the original decision to refuse the request and I am part granting one record. The basis for my decision is that I am providing you with the Code of Best Forest Practice, 2000 as the only version of this document and I am granting it in full.
Part 2: My decision is to affirm the original decision to refuse this request. The basis for my decision is that the information sought regarding: All information which relates to or has the effect of modifying the Code of Best Forest Practice in terms of amendment, supplementation or through effective removal of elements by virtue of superseding them by subsequent policy documents and technical standards and requirements is manifestly unreasonable: Article 9 (2) (a) A public authority may refuse to make available environmental information where the request is manifestly unreasonable having regard to the volume or range of information sought.
There may have been numerous policy documents and circulars which may have superseded the original code of best practice 2000 which is a 101 pages document which covers all aspects of Forestry. It would require multiple Subject Matter Experts across the Division to examine the document and identify their relevant topics, then consult any circulars that have issues in the 24 years as well as various other documents that may now supersede the original document. To note there have been 98 Forestry Circulars published from 2020 to date alone. All of these would need to be reviewed by each expert to ensure nothing of record was found in each one. One person alone in the Division could not complete this task as it involves many different areas of expertise, meaning the Division would have to allocate resources from every corner of the Division, mostly the subject matter experts. This in turn would impose a considerable burden on the DAFM Forestry Division and would result in an unreasonable diversion of resources. Narrowing the scope of your request to a particular aspect of the Code of Best Forest Practice of which you are seeking information would enable the Department to best answer your request, by allowing for efficient searching and thereby, making best use of DAFM’s resources.”
4. The Department set out details of searches conducted in relation to the request, and informed the appellant that no further records within scope of the original AIE request were located. Specifically it said, “following the assignment of this AIE request to me the following searches were undertaken to locate and retrieve the requested information: Direct contact with personnel who may have access to the information that was requested: [named officer], Assistant Principal, Approvals & AIE Unit, Forest Service; [named officer] Assistant Principal, Felling & Alleged Illegal Felling, Forest Service; [named officer], Assistant Principal, Coordination, Forest Service; [named officer], Assistant Principal, Forest Service Policy and all provided a nil return in relation to this request
.
[named officer], Forest Service Inspector, [named officer], Forest Service Senior Inspector, [named officer], Forest Service Grade 1 Inspector and [named officer], Forest Service Grade 1 Inspector and [named officer] Forestry Inspector Grade 2 all provided a nil return relation to this request.”
5. The appellant appealed to this Office on August 2024.
6. In its submission to this Office, the Department provided the following details:
“whilst the Code of Best Forest Practice, which was published in the year 2000, has in parts, been superseded by more recent policies, circulars etc, which are all available in the public domain, this has been an organic and evolving process and not one that has given rise to the creation of records.
It was confirmed that the subject matter expert in relation to this request was a named Grade 1 Inspector, Head of Environment, Forestry Division. [The named inspector] was involved in editing and coordinating the Code of Best Forest Practice when it was being published 24 years ago and he would be the Department’s foremost expert in this area. [Named inspector] has also confirmed that there is no consolidated version of the Code of Best Forest Practice which details the remaining measures that have not been superseded and the appellant is correct in his assumption that “no such document exists”.
In response to my queries on this matter, [named inspector] stated the following,
“Unfortunately it wasn’t the case that the Code was superseded section by section. In relation to afforestation, the superseding process mainly took place through the revision of the suite of environmental guidelines (for water, biodiversity, landscape, archaeology and harvesting) originally published alongside the Code. In effect, the 1st four of the original guidelines contained measures relating to afforestation. We collated these measures into a single document, rearranged, updated and added to them, resulting in the Env. Reqs. for Affor. (Dec16), which itself was recently updated under the new Programme.)”
7. I have carried out a review of this appeal under article 12(5) of the AIE Regulations. In carrying out my review, I have had regard to:
• The Guidance document provided by the Minister for the Environment, Community and Local Government on the implementation of the AIE Regulations (the Minister’s Guidance);
• Directive 2003/4/EC (the AIE Directive), upon which the AIE Regulations are based;
• The 1998 United Nations Economic Commission for Europe Convention on Access to Information, Public Participation in Decision-Making and Access to Justice in Environmental Matters (the Aarhus Convention); and
• The Aarhus Convention—An Implementation Guide (Second edition, June 2014) (‘the Aarhus Guide’).
Scope of Review
8. In accordance with article 12(5) of the AIE Regulations, my role is to review the Department’s internal review decision and to affirm, annul or vary it.
9. Regarding Part 1 of the request, the Department relies on article 7(5) on the basis that no further information is held by it. Regarding part 2, the Department has refused the request on the basis of article 9(2)(a).
10. Accordingly, the scope of this review concerns whether the Department has conducted adequate searches to identify all information within scope of Part 1 of the appellant’s request. The scope of this review also concerns whether the Department was justified in applying article 9(2)(a) to refuse Part 2 of the appellant’s request.
Analysis And Findings
Article 7(5)
11. In relation to Part 1 of the appellant’s request the Department stated “My decision is to annul the original decision to refuse the request and I am part granting one record. The basis for my decision is that I am providing you with the Code of Best Forest Practice, 2000 as the only version of this document and I am granting it in full.”
The Department states that no further information exists in relation to Part 1 of the request.
12. Article 7(5) of the AIE Regulations is the relevant provision to consider, where the question arises as to whether the requested environmental information or any further environmental information is held by or for the public authority concerned. It provides as follows;
“Where a request is made to a public authority and the information requested is not held by or for the authority concerned, that authority shall inform the applicant as soon as possible that the information is not held by or for it”.
13. This Office’s approach to dealing with this type of case is to assess whether adequate steps have been taken to identify and locate relevant environmental information, having regard to the circumstances. In determining whether the steps taken are adequate in the circumstances, a standard of reasonableness is applied. What will be considered reasonable will vary from case to case.
14. On 03 February 2026, in response to issues raised by the OCEI Investigator in this case, the Department submitted the following to this Office:
“whilst the Code of Best Forest Practice, which was published in the year 2000, has in parts, been superseded by more recent policies, circulars etc, which are all available in the public domain, this has been an organic and evolving process and not one that has given rise to the creation of records.
It was confirmed that the subject matter expert in relation to this request was [named] Grade 1 Inspector, Head of Environment, Forestry Division. [named] Grade 1 forestry inspector was involved in editing and coordinating the Code of Best Forest Practice when it was being published 24 years ago and he would be the Department’s foremost expert in this area. [named] Grade 1 inspector has also confirmed that there is no consolidated version of the Code of Best Forest Practice which details the remaining measures that have not been superseded and the appellant is correct in his assumption that “no such document exists”.
15. I am persuaded by the Department’s explanation in this case as to why the information as requested, namely the “Code of Best Forest Practice which takes account of any amendments and supplements and identifies elements that have been superseded and by what material they have been superseded”
does not exist. I also note that the Department did release in full the version of the document which it does hold.
16. I am satisfied that the Department has demonstrated that it has carried out adequate searches to locate further information within scope of the original AIE request and that no further information within scope is held by or for the Department.
Article 9(2)(a)
17. In relation to “Part 2” of the request; Article 9(2)(a) of the AIE Regulations is the relevant exemption to consider. Article 9(2)(a) of the AIE Regulations provides that a public authority may refuse to make environmental information available where the request is manifestly unreasonable having regard to the volume or range of information sought. This provision seeks to transpose Article 4(1)(b) of the AIE Directive, which provides that Member States may provide for a request for environmental information to be refused if the request is manifestly unreasonable, and, in turn, is based on part of Article 4(3)(b) of the Aarhus Convention.
18. Article 9(2)(a) of the AIE Regulations must be read alongside article 10 of the AIE Regulations. Article 10(3) of the AIE Regulations requires a public authority to consider each request on an individual basis and weigh the public interest served by disclosure against the interest served by refusal. Article 10(4) of the AIE Regulations provides that the grounds for refusal of a request shall be interpreted on a restrictive basis having regard to the public interest served by disclosure.
Meeting the Manifestly Unreasonable Threshold
19. The European Commission’s First Proposal for the AIE Directive envisaged that the exception in Article 4(1)(b) would cover requests “variously described in national legal systems as vexatious or amounting to an abus de droit.”
It noted that “compliance with certain requests could involve the public authority in disproportionate cost or effort or would obstruct or significantly interfere with the normal course of its activities. Public authorities should be able to refuse access in such cases in order to ensure their proper functioning.”
The Aarhus Convention Compliance Committee (ACCC) has emphasised that “whether or not a request is manifestly unreasonable relates to the nature of the request itself, for example, its volume, vagueness, complexity or repetitive nature, rather than the reason for the request, which is not required to be stated.”
(Report adopted on request for advice by Belarus, ACCC/A/2014/1, para. 28) .
20. In respect of a request which is voluminous or wide-ranging, within the meaning of article 9(2)(a) of the AIE Regulations, it is clear that a request is not necessarily covered by the “manifestly unreasonable”
exception just because it is voluminous or complex. Both article 7(2)(b) of the AIE Regulations and Article 3(2)(b) of the AIE Directive specifically envisage that public authorities will deal with voluminous or complex requests, albeit in a longer timeframe. I further note the parallel duty in Article 7(1) of the AIE Directive to ensure that public authorities organise environmental information with a view to its active and systematic dissemination to the public, and article 5 of the AIE Regulations which seeks to implement that provision. In his Opinion in C-217/97 Commission v Germany at paragraph 30, Advocate General Fennelly stated that the duty in Article 7 of the AIE Directive indicates that individual requests should, in principle, be on matters of detail. Accordingly, the fact that a request is detailed does not mean that it is necessarily unreasonable.
21. When considering whether a request is manifestly unreasonable, it is necessary to examine the impact on the public authority of dealing with the request. In particular, I must examine whether responding to the request would involve the public authority in disproportionate cost or effort, or would obstruct or significantly interfere with the normal course of its activities. In light of the findings of the Court of Justice of the European Union in T-2/03 Verein für Konsumenten information v. Commission, at paragraphs 101-115, I consider that the exception in article 9(2)(a) is only available where the administrative burden entailed by dealing with the request is particularly heavy. The burden is on the public authority to demonstrate the unreasonableness of the task entailed by the request. I expect that if a public authority wishes to rely on the manifestly unreasonable nature of a request, that public authority will clearly demonstrate the actual and specific impact that dealing with the request would have on its normal activities.
22. Furthermore, in every case, regard should be had to the purpose of the AIE Regime, as reflected in Recital 1 of the Preamble 6 to the AIE Directive, which provides that “increased public access to environmental information and the dissemination of such information contribute to greater public awareness of environmental decision-making and, eventually, to a better environment.”
Accordingly, in cases involving article 9(2)(a) this Office may consider whether the information requested is the kind of environmental information that one would expect to be organised by the public authority in a manner that enables its easy dissemination.
23. Having considered the volume, range and type of information requested in this case, I do note that any circulars which supersede the code of best forest practice since it was first published 26 years ago, are easily accessible and publicly available on the
Forestry Circulars page
on Gov.ie , and I do not consider the other information sought to be of the type that one would expect to be organised by the public authority in a manner that enables its easy dissemination.
24. I am also persuaded by the arguments put forward by the Department as to why the request is manifestly unreasonable having regard to the volume or range of information sought. The Department submits that: “There may have been numerous policy documents and circulars which may have superseded the original code of best practice 2000 which is a 101 pages document which covers all aspects of Forestry. It would require multiple Subject Matter Experts across the Division to examine the document and identify their relevant topics, then consult any circulars that have issued in the 24 years as well as various other documents that may now supersede the original document. To note there have been 98 Forestry Circulars published from 2020 to date alone. All of these would need to be reviewed by each expert to ensure nothing of record was found in each one. One person alone in the Division could not complete this task as it involves many different areas of expertise, meaning the Division would have to allocate resources from every corner of the Division, mostly the subject matter experts. This in turn would impose a considerable burden on the DAFM Forestry Division and would result in an unreasonable diversion of resources.”
25. Part 2 of the appellant’s request seeks all information having a modifying or superseding effect on the Code. Based on my consideration of the Department’s submission, I consider processing this part of the request would require the Department to assess a large body of material and determine its legal or practical relationship with the Code. I have had regard in this case to the volume and the range of information sought, the nature of the information requested, the task that the Department submits it must undertake to identify it, and the impact of dealing with the request on the Department’s other functions. Taking all of the above into account, I am satisfied that this request meets the manifestly unreasonable threshold.
Article 10 of the AIE Regulations
26. Although I have found article 9(2)(a) of the AIE Regulations applies, I must weigh the public interest served by disclosure against the interest served by refusal as is required by articles 10(3) and 10(4) of the AIE Regulations. In considering the public interest served by disclosure, it is important to be mindful of the purpose of the AIE regime, as reflected in Recital 1 of the Preamble to the AIE Directive, which provides that “increased public access to environmental information and the dissemination of such information contribute to greater public awareness of environmental decision-making and, eventually to a better environment.”
The AIE regime thereby recognises a very strong public interest in openness and transparency in relation to environmental decision-making.
27. The AIE regime also acknowledges that there may be exceptions to the general rule of disclosure of information, as noted in Recital 16 of the AIE Directive, which provides that “public authorities should be permitted to refuse a request for environmental information in specific and clearly defined cases.”
One such case is where the request is manifestly unreasonable having regard to the volume or range of information sought. The public interest in maintaining the exception lies in ensuring that the processing of AIE Requests does not cause an unreasonable interference and/or disruption of the work of a public authority.
28. I am satisfied that attempting to identify and compile the information requested in Part 2 would place a significant administrative burden on the Department and would impact its ability to carry out its core functions. I am further satisfied that any public interest in disclosure of the information at issue does not outweigh the interest served by refusal.
Decision
29. Having carried out a review under article 12(5) of the AIE Regulations, I affirm the Department’s decision. In respect of Part 1 of the request, I am satisfied that the Department released the Code of Best Forest Practice, 2000, and that no further relevant information within the scope of Part 1 is held by or for the Department.
30. In respect of Part 2 of the request, I am satisfied that the Department was justified in refusing the request under article 9(2)(a) of the AIE Regulations on the basis that it was manifestly unreasonable having regard to the volume and range of information sought.
Appeal to the High Court
31. A party to the appeal or any other person affected by this decision may appeal to the High Court on a point of law from the decision. Such an appeal must be initiated not later than two months after notice of the decision was given to the person bringing the appeal.
Ger Deering
Commissioner for Environmental Information
respondent: Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine
